name: Face Replacement and Digital Doubles
title: Face Replacement and Digital Doubles
answer: Face replacement and digital doubles cover the work of putting one performer's face onto another body, or building a synthetic performer that stands in for a real one across a shot, a scene or an entire production. The practice spans de-ageing a lead actor, doubling a stunt performer for a dangerous sequence, and creating a fully digital character where no living performer appears on set. It sits inside cinematography and video synthesis because the output has to cut together with photographed footage, matching lens, light and movement rather than standing alone as a clip.

sections.body: Face replacement and digital doubles cover the work of putting one performer's face onto another body, or building a synthetic performer that stands in for a real one across a shot, a scene or an entire production. The practice spans de-ageing a lead actor, doubling a stunt performer for a dangerous sequence, and creating a fully digital character where no living performer appears on set. It sits inside cinematography and video synthesis because the output has to cut together with photographed footage, matching lens, light and movement rather than standing alone as a clip.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a pipeline rather than a single model: tracking and reconstruction tools to recover a face's shape and motion, a synthesis stage that renders the replacement, and a compositing stage that puts it back into the plate. Studios use a mix of commercial packages and in-house systems, and the same tasks increasingly appear in general video models among the 1,000 video models this site tracks. Compute is the practical constraint, since a shot may need many passes at high resolution before it is usable, and review happens on workstations rather than in a browser.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical job starts with reference capture of the source performer, often a dedicated pass with multiple cameras and controlled lighting, plus a clean plate of the scene. Artists then solve the head pose and expression over time, retarget that motion onto the target face, and render the result with the scene's lighting baked in. The hard part is not the still frame but the performance: micro-expressions, eye direction, lip sync and the small instabilities that make a face read as alive. Supervisors review iterations against the original take, and the final pass is graded and matched to the surrounding footage.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Consent is the central issue, because a digital double can outlive the agreement that created it and can be reused in material the performer never saw. Contracts now commonly specify the term, the productions covered, and who holds the scan data, and unions have pushed for notification and payment when a double is used. Where a face is recognisable, publicity and personality rights apply alongside copyright, and this site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits as a rough measure of how contested these questions have become. Provenance matters too: studios keep records of which shots are synthetic, and watermarking and signed capture logs are used to show where a frame came from.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward doubles built once and reused across a franchise, with the scan and the performance model treated as a production asset rather than a per-shot expense. Real-time rendering is closing the gap with offline pipelines, which changes how a director can work with a synthetic performer on set. At the same time, the legal and ethical frame is still forming, and the terms under which a performer's likeness can be stored, retrained and reanimated are likely to be settled in contracts and courtrooms rather than in the tools themselves.
